text: In 1859, the United States and the British Empire brought warships, cannons and thousands of men to one small island.
They were ready to go to war.
Over a pig.
I'm Sir Digsworth, and this is the Pig War.
The trouble starts with a treaty. In 1846, Britain and America agree on a border: down the middle of the channel.
Unfortunately, there are two channels. And between them sit the San Juan Islands.
So both countries say the islands are theirs.
On San Juan Island, the British Hudson's Bay Company runs a sheep farm. Its manager, Charles Griffin, lets his pigs wander wherever they like.
Then American settlers arrive. One of them is a farmer from Kentucky, called Lyman Cutlar. He plants potatoes.
On the 15th of June, 1859, Cutlar finds a pig in his garden, eating his potatoes. Not for the first time.
So he shoots it.
The pig belongs to Griffin.
Cutlar offers him 10 dollars. Griffin demands 100.
The story goes that Cutlar said: it was eating my potatoes. And Griffin replied: it is up to you to keep your potatoes out of my pig.
The British threaten to arrest Cutlar. So the American settlers ask for the army.
The army sends Captain George Pickett, with 66 soldiers.
Pickett says: we'll make a Bunker Hill of it.
The British answer with 3 warships.
Then both sides send more. By August, 461 Americans with 14 cannons are facing 5 warships, with 70 guns and 2,140 men.
The Americans build a fort. The young officer in charge, Henry Robert, will later write Robert's Rules of Order: a famous guide to holding a polite meeting.
The British governor orders his navy to push the Americans off the island.
Then Rear Admiral Robert Baynes arrives, and refuses. He will not start a war between two great nations over a squabble about a pig.
In September, President James Buchanan sends General Winfield Scott to negotiate.
The two sides make a deal. Each will keep no more than 100 men on the island, until somebody decides who owns it.
The British camp at the north end. The Americans camp at the south.
And there they stay, for 12 years.
The two camps visit each other on national holidays. They hold sports competitions.
Park rangers say the biggest threat to peace was the amount of alcohol on the island.
Finally, the question is handed to a referee: the German emperor, Wilhelm the First.
In October 1872, he decides. The islands are American.
A month later, the British marines sail home.
The Pig War lasted 13 years. Total casualties: one pig.
Today the island is a national park. And the British flag still flies over the old British camp. It is raised every day, by American park rangers.
Not bad, for a war that started in a potato patch.
I'm Sir Digsworth. Do mind the pig.
